tea.title: One word, two roads
tea.blurb: Almost every language calls tea either something like te or something like cha — depending on whether it arrived by sea or by land.
tea.chapters[0].title: One leaf, two sounds
tea.chapters[0].body: Tea comes from China, but as the word travelled the world it settled into just two shapes: something like te, or something like cha. Both are Chinese — Min Nan says tê, Mandarin and Cantonese say chá. What decided between them was the port, and the road, the leaves left by.
tea.chapters[1].title: By sea: te
tea.chapters[1].body: In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company dominated the sea trade in tea. Buying from Hokkien merchants on the Fujian coast and in Batavia (now Jakarta), the Dutch picked up the word tê — and carried it on their ships to Amsterdam, then London, Paris and Berlin.
tea.chapters[2].title: By land: cha
tea.chapters[2].body: Overland, tea went west and north along the Silk Road and the Tea Horse Road, carrying the northern sound cha: Persian chāy, Arabic shāy, Turkish çay, Russian chay (чай) — and, through Indian Ocean traders, Swahili chai in East Africa.
tea.chapters[3].title: The exception: Portugal
tea.chapters[3].body: The Portuguese came by sea too — so why chá? Their foothold in China was Macau, where people speak Cantonese. Japanese and Korean say cha as well: tea reached them much earlier, with monks and envoys. And one well-hidden case: Polish herbata comes from Latin herba thea, “tea herb” — te is tucked inside.
tea.chapters[4].title: One map, two histories
tea.chapters[4].body: Put every te and every cha together and you get a map of trade history: coasts and western Europe say te, the interior and the Islamic world say cha. The next time you ask for tea, the syllable you use is an echo of a ship or a caravan, centuries ago.
tea.chapters[4].source: After Östen Dahl, “Tea”, chapter 138 of the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS).
people.title: The people behind the languages
people.kicker: Inventors, decipherers, revivers — and last speakers
people.blurb: A king who made an alphabet for his people, a silversmith who could not read who made a script for his, a man who turned an ancient language back into a mother tongue… Sometimes a language’s fate rests on one person.
people.chapters[0].title: A king’s twenty-eight letters
people.chapters[0].body: In fifteenth-century Korea, writing meant Classical Chinese, and only a small elite could read and write. In 1443 King Sejong of Joseon and his scholars created a new alphabet, promulgated in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, “the correct sounds for the instruction of the people”. His preface explains why: the sounds of the language differ from Chinese, so many ordinary people had things to say but no way to write them; “feeling compassion, I have newly made twenty-eight letters, which I wish everyone to learn easily for daily use.” The consonants sketch the organs of speech: ㄱ the tongue root blocking the throat, ㄴ the tongue against the roof of the mouth, ㅁ the shape of the mouth. Today the alphabet is called Hangul (Chosŏn’gŭl in the North).
people.chapters[0].portrait.caption: A page of the Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446) explaining the letters
people.chapters[1].title: The man who could not read
people.chapters[1].body: Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith who could not read or write any language. Seeing settlers put speech on paper, he was convinced his people could do the same. After some twelve years of trying, in 1821 he completed a syllabary: one symbol for each syllable, 86 in all (85 are used today). Some look like English letters but sound nothing like them: Ꭱ, like an R, is e; Ꮋ, like an H, is mi; Ꮪ, like an S, is du. A Cherokee speaker could learn it in weeks, and it spread quickly; in 1828 the first Cherokee newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, began printing. A person who could not read inventing a writing system on his own is almost without parallel in history.
people.chapters[1].portrait.caption: Sequoyah with his syllabary, by Henry Inman, c. 1830
people.chapters[2].title: Fourteen centuries of silence
people.chapters[2].body: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in AD 394; after that, the knowledge of how to read it faded away. In 1799 French soldiers in Egypt found a stone at Rosetta bearing one decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. The key lay with a young French scholar, Jean-François Champollion, who had studied Coptic — the last stage of the Egyptian language, still used in the liturgy of the Coptic Church — since his teens. In a royal cartouche from a temple he recognised the sun sign as ra (Coptic “sun” is rē) and the next sign as ms (Coptic “to give birth” is mise): the name was Ramesses. He announced the decipherment in 1822. The story goes that he ran into his brother’s office, cried “I’ve got it!” and fainted.
people.chapters[2].portrait.caption: Champollion, by Léon Cogniet, 1831
people.chapters[3].title: A mother tongue again
people.chapters[3].body: Somewhere between the 2nd and 4th centuries AD Hebrew stopped being anyone’s mother tongue, though it lived on for well over a thousand years in prayer and in writing. In 1881 Eliezer Ben-Yehuda moved to Jerusalem and resolved to speak only Hebrew at home; his son became the first child in modern times to grow up with Hebrew as his first language. To let an ancient language talk about modern life he compiled a vast dictionary and coined words such as milon (dictionary) and iton (newspaper); the dictionary was completed only in 1959, decades after his death. He did not do it alone — schools and new communities mattered as much — but he became the face of what is often called the most successful language revival in history. Today Hebrew has millions of native speakers.
people.chapters[3].portrait.caption: Ben-Yehuda at his desk in Jerusalem, c. 1912
people.chapters[4].title: Doctor Hopeful
people.chapters[4].body: Zamenhof grew up in Białystok, then in the Russian Empire, a town where Poles, Russians, Germans and Jews each kept to their own language and eyed one another with suspicion. He believed a neutral language belonging to everyone could ease such divides. In 1887 he published a small book presenting his international language under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto — “Doctor One-who-hopes” — and the name stuck to the language. Its grammar fits in sixteen rules, with no irregular verbs. It never became humanity’s second language, but for well over a century people have spoken and written it, and about a thousand have even grown up with it as a mother tongue.
people.chapters[4].portrait.caption: Zamenhof, c. 1905
people.chapters[5].title: Another king, another script
people.chapters[5].body: At the end of the nineteenth century, in the Bamum kingdom of what is now western Cameroon, the young King Ibrahim Njoya set out to design a script for his language. The first version had hundreds of picture-like signs; revised again and again, by around 1910 it had become a syllabary of some 80 signs. He used it to record the kingdom’s history, customs and medicine, and opened schools in his capital, Foumban, to teach it. Cameroon was then under colonial rule, first German, later French. In 1931 the French authorities deposed him and exiled him to Yaoundé, where he died two years later, and the script fell out of use. Today the manuscripts kept at the palace are being catalogued, and in 2009 the Bamum script was added to Unicode.
people.chapters[5].portrait.caption: King Njoya, early twentieth century
people.chapters[6].title: The last of the Yahi
people.chapters[6].body: After the California Gold Rush, settlers and militias all but wiped out the Yahi; the few survivors hid in the hills for some forty years. In August 1911 the last of them, starving, walked out of the forest and was found at a slaughterhouse near Oroville. He spent the rest of his life at an anthropology museum in San Francisco, recording the words, stories and songs of Yahi — a dialect of Yana — with the anthropologist Alfred Kroeber and the linguist Edward Sapir. Following Yahi custom he never spoke his own name, so he was called Ishi: “man” in his language. He died of tuberculosis in 1916.
people.chapters[6].portrait.caption: Ishi, 1911
people.chapters[7].title: The code that was never broken
people.chapters[7].body: In the Second World War the US Marine Corps recruited some four hundred Navajo men to send messages in their language across the Pacific. Navajo was then barely written down and was built utterly unlike English or Japanese — and on top of it they devised a code: a tank was a “tortoise”, a submarine an “iron fish”, a fighter plane a “hummingbird”. It was never broken. In the first two days at Iwo Jima six Navajo code talkers sent and received more than eight hundred messages without a single error. Many of them had been punished as children, at boarding school, for speaking Navajo. Their story stayed classified until 1968.
people.chapters[7].source: Code words as spelled in the declassified Navajo Code Talkers’ Dictionary.
people.chapters[7].portrait.caption: Navajo code talkers Preston and Frank Toledo, 1943
people.chapters[8].title: The last speaker
people.chapters[8].body: Cristina Calderón lived on Navarino Island at the southern tip of Chile and was the last native speaker of Yaghan, the language of the canoe people who for generations travelled the channels of Tierra del Fuego. In her last years she worked with her granddaughter on a vocabulary and a book of stories, setting down everything she remembered. She died in February 2022, aged 93. Every language that falls silent has a last speaker like her — and most of the time, no one writes down their name.
people.chapters[8].portrait.caption: Cristina Calderón, 2013
people.chapters[9].title: The last, and the first
people.chapters[9].body: The last native speaker of Manx, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. Before he did, recordings were made of him and the island’s other elders, and with those recordings and old books a band of learners carried the language on. In 2001 the Isle of Man opened a primary school taught entirely in Manx, and there are now children growing up speaking it: a new first generation. (This atlas follows Glottolog, which still lists Manx as extinct in the traditional sense of a mother tongue passed down; UNESCO reclassified it as critically endangered in 2009.)
untranslatable.title: The “untranslatable” words
untranslatable.kicker: saudade, hygge, komorebi — and the myths that travel with them
untranslatable.blurb: Some words take a whole sentence to explain in another language. They are not truly untranslatable — but they show what a culture thought worth a word of its own.
untranslatable.chapters[0].title: The many shapes of longing
untranslatable.chapters[0].body: Portuguese saudade is often called the most Portuguese of words: a longing for someone or something absent, perhaps never to return, sweet and sad at once. Welsh hiraeth is a yearning for home — a home you may not be able to return to, or that perhaps never was. Nabokov wrote that no single English word renders all the shades of Russian тоска (toska): at its deepest a spiritual anguish without cause, lower down “a longing with nothing to long for”, and at its lowest plain boredom.
untranslatable.chapters[0].table.rows[0]: longing for someone or something absent, perhaps never to return
untranslatable.chapters[0].table.rows[1]: yearning for a home you cannot return to
untranslatable.chapters[0].table.rows[2]: an ache of the soul, often without a cause
untranslatable.chapters[0].table.rows[3]: an intense yearning for something far off or out of reach
untranslatable.chapters[1].title: Cosy, and just enough
untranslatable.chapters[1].body: Danish hygge has lately conquered the world: candlelight, a warm drink, the snug ease of being with people you are close to. Dutch gezellig is similar, with a little more bustle — a room, a party or a person can all be gezellig. Swedish lagom means “not too much, not too little: just right”. The internet likes to say it comes from Vikings passing a drinking horn “around the team” (laget om); that is folk etymology — it comes from Old Swedish lag, “law”, as in “the amount custom allows”. Swedes also have fika: stopping for coffee and something sweet with colleagues or friends, a word made by turning an old word for coffee, kaffi, back to front.
untranslatable.chapters[1].table.rows[1]: cosy, convivial, good to be in
untranslatable.chapters[1].table.rows[2]: not too much, not too little
untranslatable.chapters[1].table.rows[3]: a break for coffee, something sweet and company
untranslatable.chapters[2].title: Between people
untranslatable.chapters[2].body: Korean 눈치 (nunchi, literally “eye-measure”) is the knack of reading a room: sensing the mood the moment you walk in, knowing what to say and what to leave unsaid. Persian تعارف (taarof) is an etiquette of courtesy: the host insists, the guest declines, the shopkeeper may even say there is nothing to pay — and both sides know it is a ritual. In Zulu and the other Nguni languages of southern Africa, ubuntu is the idea that we become ourselves through others: “a person is a person through other people”. Chinese 缘分 (yuánfèn), the bond of chance or fate that brings two people together, takes a sentence to explain in most languages. And Tagalog kilig — the giddy flutter when the person you like so much as glances at you — entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2016.
untranslatable.chapters[2].table.rows[0]: the knack of sensing the mood and what others think
untranslatable.chapters[2].table.rows[1]: the ritual of polite offering and refusing
untranslatable.chapters[2].table.rows[2]: humanity towards others: a person is a person through other people
untranslatable.chapters[2].table.rows[3]: the chance or fate that brings people together
untranslatable.chapters[2].table.rows[4]: the giddy rush of romantic excitement
untranslatable.chapters[3].title: Words for everyday life
untranslatable.chapters[3].body: Spanish sobremesa is the time after a meal when no one hurries to leave the table and the talk goes on — sometimes longer than the meal itself. Japanese 積ん読 (tsundoku), a word from the Meiji era, fuses “leave piled up” (tsunde oku) with “reading” (dokusho): books bought, stacked ever higher, never read. In Indonesia, jam karet is “rubber time”: appointments that stretch. And Hindi जुगाड़ (jugaad) is a clever, make-do fix out of whatever is to hand.
untranslatable.chapters[3].table.rows[0]: lingering at the table after a meal, talking
untranslatable.chapters[3].table.rows[1]: buying books and letting them pile up unread
untranslatable.chapters[3].table.rows[3]: a clever improvised fix with whatever is at hand
untranslatable.chapters[4].title: A picture in a word
untranslatable.chapters[4].body: Japanese 木漏れ日 (komorebi) is sunlight dappling through the leaves of trees. Turkish yakamoz is the glitter of light on the sea at night — the glow of tiny bioluminescent plankton, or the path the moon lays across the water. And Finnish has an old measure of distance, poronkusema, literally “reindeer’s pee”: how far a reindeer could pull a sledge before it had to stop to relieve itself, about seven and a half kilometres.
untranslatable.chapters[4].table.rows[1]: sparkles of light on the sea at night, or moonlight on the water
untranslatable.chapters[4].table.rows[2]: how far a reindeer goes without a break, about 7.5 km
untranslatable.chapters[5].title: Beware the lists
untranslatable.chapters[5].body: “The Inuit have a hundred words for snow” is perhaps the most widespread of all language legends. It goes back to a passage by the anthropologist Franz Boas in 1911, which gave just four roots: snow on the ground, falling snow, drifting snow and a snowdrift. Retold again and again, the count swelled to dozens, then hundreds. Inuit languages glue many pieces into one long word, so “how many words” is hard to count in the first place — and English has snow, sleet, slush, blizzard and more. Another regular is mamihlapinatapai from Yaghan in Tierra del Fuego, said to mean “a look between two people, each hoping the other will offer to do what both want but neither will begin”, and named by Guinness the most succinct word. That gloss comes from a nineteenth-century missionary’s dictionary, and its exact sense is still debated. In the end, anything can be said in any language; what these words show is what a culture found worth a name of its own.
untranslatable.chapters[5].table.rows[4]: (reputedly) a look shared by two, each waiting for the other to begin
untranslatable.chapters[5].source: The four snow roots are from Boas’s introduction to the Handbook of American Indian Languages (1911).
austronesian.title: A family written by canoes
austronesian.blurb: Setting out from Taiwan, across the Pacific and the Indian Ocean — long before Columbus, Austronesian speakers had carried their languages over half the globe.
austronesian.chapters[0].title: Where it began: Taiwan
austronesian.chapters[0].body: Austronesian has some 1,250 languages, but its oldest and most diverse branches are all in Taiwan: Amis, Atayal, Paiwan, Bunun… Linguists reason that a family’s homeland is usually where it is most diverse. Some four thousand years ago and more, Austronesian speakers began moving south from Taiwan.
austronesian.chapters[1].title: From island to island
austronesian.chapters[1].body: They reached the Philippines first, then pushed south into Borneo, Sulawesi and Java, and east to the Marianas. Tagalog, Malay, Indonesian and Javanese all descend from these movements.
austronesian.chapters[2].title: Across the Indian Ocean
austronesian.chapters[2].body: More than a thousand years ago, seafarers from southeastern Borneo sailed west across the entire Indian Ocean to Madagascar, off Africa. That is why Malagasy’s closest relative is not in Africa but in Borneo, some 7,000 km away: Ma’anyan.
austronesian.chapters[3].title: The last ocean
austronesian.chapters[3].body: Around three thousand years ago Lapita voyagers reached Remote Oceania — Fiji, Tonga, Samoa. Nearly two thousand years later Polynesians, navigating double-hulled canoes by stars, swells and birds, found Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand, among the last large lands people settled.
austronesian.chapters[4].title: “Five” and “hand”
austronesian.chapters[4].body: Proto-Austronesian *lima meant both “five” and “hand”. Thousands of years later, from Taiwan to Hawaii, people still count to five this way. Tahitian is the exception: the old word is said to have fallen under a naming taboo and was replaced by pae.
austronesian.chapters[4].table.caption: “five”
indo-european.title: From Sanskrit to English
indo-european.blurb: In 1786 a British judge in India noticed that Sanskrit words for father, mother and three looked strikingly like Latin.
indo-european.chapters[0].title: Calcutta, 1786
indo-european.chapters[0].body: Studying Sanskrit in Calcutta, William Jones found it resembled Greek and Latin too closely for chance: all three must have “sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists”. That source came to be called Proto-Indo-European.
indo-european.chapters[0].table.caption: “mother”
indo-european.chapters[1].title: Grimm’s law
indo-european.chapters[1].body: Why does Latin pater, piscis, pēs line up with English father, fish, foot? In 1822 Jacob Grimm — the elder of the fairy-tale brothers — set out the rule: the Germanic languages turned Proto-Indo-European *p into f, *t into th, *k into h. Sound change, it turned out, is regular.
indo-european.chapters[2].title: A homeland on the steppe
indo-european.chapters[2].body: Proto-Indo-European was spoken roughly six to five thousand years ago. The prevailing “steppe hypothesis” puts its speakers north of the Black and Caspian Seas, spreading with the horse and the wheeled wagon; the rival “Anatolian hypothesis” has it spreading with early farming from present-day Turkey. Ancient DNA has lately favoured the steppe.
indo-european.chapters[3].title: The easternmost, the oldest
indo-european.chapters[3].body: The family reached further than you might think. Tocharian, its easternmost branch, was spoken in the oasis cities of Xinjiang and left Buddhist manuscripts; Hittite, the oldest attested, was pressed into Anatolian clay over three thousand years ago. Both are extinct — and both are crucial to reconstructing the parent language.
indo-european.chapters[4].title: Across the oceans
indo-european.chapters[4].body: Today about four in ten people speak an Indo-European language natively — largely the work of the last five hundred years, as English, Spanish, Portuguese and French crossed the oceans with colonial expansion, crowding out thousands of local languages.
africa.title: Clicks, tones and the Bantu journey
africa.blurb: Africa has more than two thousand languages, nearly a third of the world’s. It has the most varied sounds on Earth, and a migration that remade half a continent.
africa.chapters[0].title: A third of all languages
africa.chapters[0].body: Glottolog records {africa} languages in Africa. In the 1960s Joseph Greenberg sorted them into four great families; today only Afro-Asiatic and the core of his Niger-Congo (Atlantic-Congo) are widely accepted, while “Nilo-Saharan” and “Khoisan” are seen as collections of independent families and isolates.
africa.chapters[1].title: The Bantu journey
africa.chapters[1].body: Some three to four thousand years ago, Bantu-speaking people began moving out from the borderlands of present-day Cameroon and Nigeria, east and south, until they covered much of the continent. The resemblances among today’s roughly five hundred Bantu languages — Swahili, Zulu, Shona, Lingala… — are the footprints of that journey.
africa.chapters[2].title: Noun classes
africa.chapters[2].body: Bantu languages have no masculine or feminine — instead they sort nouns into a dozen or more classes, each with its own prefix, and the other words in a sentence agree with it. In Swahili a person is mtu and people watu; a book is kitabu and books vitabu.
africa.chapters[3].title: Clicks
africa.chapters[3].body: In southern Africa some languages use clicks — the sounds of the tongue snapping off the roof of the mouth — as ordinary consonants. Khoekhoe, ǃXóõ and their neighbours (once lumped together as “Khoisan”) have dozens of them; so do Hadza and Sandawe in Tanzania, both isolates. Zulu and Xhosa borrowed their clicks from these neighbours after Bantu speakers moved south.
africa.chapters[4].title: Drums that talk
africa.chapters[4].body: Most African languages are tonal. Yoruba distinguishes high, mid and low tones, and the same string of syllables on a different melody is a different word. That is why Yoruba “talking drums” can imitate the rise and fall of a sentence and beat out speech that listeners understand.
americas.title: Before Columbus
americas.blurb: When Europeans arrived, the Americas held more than a thousand languages in well over a hundred unrelated families. Many are still spoken; many have fallen silent.
americas.chapters[0].title: More than a hundred families
americas.chapters[0].body: Glottolog records {americas} languages across North and South America. In variety of families the Americas are among the richest places on Earth: from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, well over a hundred families and isolates with no demonstrable relationship to one another.
americas.chapters[1].title: The language of the Inca
americas.chapters[1].body: Quechua — Runa Simi, “the people’s language” — was the lingua franca of the Inca Empire, which kept its records on knotted cords called khipu. Today the Quechuan languages have millions of speakers along the Andes from Colombia to Argentina, the most widely spoken indigenous languages of the Americas.
americas.chapters[2].title: Written in stone
americas.chapters[2].body: Maya script is the only pre-Columbian writing system of the Americas to have been largely deciphered — a breakthrough of the late twentieth century, after the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov showed that it recorded syllables as well as words. Several million people still speak some thirty Mayan languages, among them K’iche’ and Yucatec.
americas.chapters[3].title: Tomatoes and chillies
americas.chapters[3].body: The Aztec Empire spoke Nahuatl. The Spanish carried away not only its crops but their names: tomato (from tomatl), avocado (āhuacatl), chilli (chīlli), coyote (coyōtl). Over a million people still speak varieties of Nahuatl today.
americas.chapters[4].title: Voices of the north
americas.chapters[4].body: In North America, Navajo became an unbreakable code in the Second World War; the Cherokee Sequoyah invented a script single-handed; Inuktitut in Canada is written in a syllabary first devised by missionaries. But many of the continent’s languages — California alone had around a hundred — are gone, or spoken only by a few elders.
isolates.title: Languages without relatives
isolates.blurb: Most languages have hundreds of relatives. A few have none anywhere in the world.
isolates.chapters[0].title: The orphan of the Pyrenees
isolates.chapters[0].body: Basque is ringed by Indo-European — Spanish, French, Gascon — and related to none of them. It is very likely the last survivor of the languages of western Europe before Indo-European arrived. Its numbers show how much it stands apart.
isolates.chapters[1].title: Among the mountains
isolates.chapters[1].body: In the Karakoram valleys of northern Pakistan, Burushaski is surrounded by Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan and Turkic — and kin to none of them. Mountains and valleys are often refuges for old languages.
isolates.chapters[2].title: Alone on clay
isolates.chapters[2].body: Sumerian, one of humanity’s first written languages, is also an isolate. We know it only because Mesopotamians pressed it into clay five thousand years ago; countless other isolates vanished without a trace.
isolates.chapters[3].title: Scattered across the world
isolates.chapters[3].body: Glottolog lists {isolates} isolates, on almost every continent and especially in the Americas and New Guinea. Each counts as a family of one — in the forest of languages, a lone tree.
sinitic.title: Chinese is not one language
sinitic.blurb: People from Shanghai, Guangzhou and Xiamen may not understand each other’s home speech at all. To a linguist these are different languages in one family.
sinitic.chapters[0].title: A family
sinitic.chapters[0].body: To linguists, “Chinese” is less a language than a branch: Mandarin, Wu, Yue, Min, Hakka, Xiang, Gan… often further apart than Spanish and Italian. What binds them is a common ancestor and a shared written language.
sinitic.chapters[1].title: The same character, 人
sinitic.chapters[1].body: Written the same, spoken differently. The differences follow strict correspondences — and those regular patterns are what let linguists reason back to the common ancestor: Middle Chinese, and before it Old Chinese.
sinitic.chapters[1].table.caption: 人 “person”
sinitic.chapters[2].title: The vanished checked tone
sinitic.chapters[2].body: Middle Chinese had many syllables ending in -p, -t or -k — the “entering tone”. Northern Mandarin lost them around the Yuan dynasty; Cantonese kept them all. That is why some Tang poems rhyme better read in Cantonese than in Mandarin.
sinitic.chapters[3].title: Across the southern seas
sinitic.chapters[3].body: Min is thought to be the earliest branch to split from the rest of Sinitic. From the Ming and Qing dynasties on, Hokkien and Hakka emigrants settled across Southeast Asia, so Min Nan took root in Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines; Taiwanese is Min Nan too. English tea set out from here.
sinitic.chapters[4].title: The neighbours of Chinese
sinitic.chapters[4].body: Around the Sinitic languages live many unrelated families: other Sino-Tibetan languages such as Tibetan and Yi; Kra-Dai languages such as Zhuang and Kam; Hmong-Mien; Turkic Uyghur and Kazakh; Mongolian; Tungusic; Austroasiatic Wa; even Indo-European Sarikoli. Many of them are quietly fading.
endangered.title: Voices growing faint
endangered.blurb: Every few months a language may lose its last native speaker. But some languages have come back from the dead.
endangered.chapters[0].title: Half of all languages
endangered.chapters[0].body: Of the {total} languages on this globe, {endangered} are endangered to some degree and {extinct} are already extinct (the hollow dots). The darker the colour, the closer a language is to falling silent.
endangered.chapters[1].title: Australia
endangered.chapters[1].body: Australia had about 250 languages when Europeans arrived; only a dozen or so are still learned by children. With them go distinctive ways of thinking — Guugu Yimithirr, for one, barely uses “left” and “right”, placing everything by compass direction.
endangered.chapters[2].title: Close to home
endangered.chapters[2].body: In East Asia, Manchu was once the official language of an empire and now has a handful of native speakers; Ainu in Hokkaido survives with very few elders. Language loss is usually quiet: parents stop speaking it to their children, and a generation later it lives only in recordings.
endangered.chapters[3].title: Languages that came back
endangered.chapters[3].body: Loss is not always final. Hebrew became an everyday language again after nearly two thousand years without native speakers; Hawaiian and Māori returned to children through “language nest” preschools; Cornish and Manx were reawakened even after being declared extinct.
endangered.chapters[4].title: Seven thousand ways of seeing
endangered.chapters[4].body: Every language is a way of seeing the world: how to count, give directions, name your kin, tell a joke. You may never learn most of them — but knowing they exist is itself a kind of care. Turn the globe and look somewhere you have never heard of.
